prompt: Start the deck: FinBridge board strategy review, Q3 2026. Subtitle along the lines of 'where we win in UK SME spend management'.
why: First slide of the deck; guide rule 1.

prompt: First slide for the NHS trust outpatient backlog diagnostic we present to the exec committee next week. It's a ~40-slide pack; open with the title and our one-line answer.
why: It is the first slide, so rule 1 wins before the long-deck section rule.

prompt: We're 12 slides into the retail network review and now moving to part 3, store format options. Need the slide that opens that part.
why: Start of a new part in a 12+ slide deck; rule 2.

prompt: Next up in the 25-slide logistics deck is the cost-to-serve deep dive. Mark the start of that chapter.
why: Opens a new part of a long deck; rule 2.

prompt: Slide 18 of ~30 in the HR transformation pack: this is where 'Part 4: Making it happen' begins.
why: Part divider mid-way through a long deck; rule 2.

prompt: Slide arguing that UK SMEs lose real money to manual expense reconciliation. Our survey says the average SME spends £11,400 a year in finance staff time on it.
why: A short argument proven by one number; rule 3.

prompt: I need to convince the board the addressable market is big enough: UK SMEs with 10-249 employees put £84bn a year through business cards. That's the point of the slide.
why: One market-size number proves the argument; rule 3.

prompt: Churn slide for the SaaS review. The story: 62% of churned accounts never activated an integration. NPS is 41 and support tickets are up 12%, but the activation stat is the story.
why: User singles out one decisive number; other stats are context, so rule 3 over cards.

prompt: Make the case that the council's temp-agency spend is out of control: £23.6m last year against a £9m budget.
why: The argument rests on one gap (a £14.6m overspend), so one decisive number; rule 3.

prompt: Revenue trend for the FinBridge board. Monthly card spend processed (£m): Jan 18, Feb 19, Mar 22, Apr 21, May 26, Jun 31, Jul 30, Aug 36. Need to explain the June jump (Xero integration launch) and the July dip (seasonality).
why: A time series with specific points to pin and explain; rule 4.

prompt: Show how our churn cohort curves differ: the 2024 cohorts retain much better after month 3, and I want to call out why (onboarding redesign, shift to annual plans).
why: Series whose meaning depends on 2 explanatory observations the chart cannot show; rule 4.

prompt: UK grocery market share 2019-2025, discounters vs the big four. Point out the year they cross over and the two drivers behind it.
why: Crossover calls for a chart, and the drivers are notes the chart does not show; rule 4.

prompt: A&E performance across our 12 trusts, % seen within 4 hours. I want to flag the three outliers and what they have in common.
why: Comparison of sizes over categories with outliers to pin and explain; rule 4 comes before the >6-row table rule.

prompt: How gross margin went from 38% to 31%: interchange cut -3pts, fraud losses -2, FX mix -1.5, pricing +0.5, other -1. Explain each of the big drivers briefly.
why: A bridge over categories that needs observations per driver; rule 4.

prompt: Client emissions by scope, 2020-2025. The board must see scope 3 is 80% and growing, and that scope 1-2 progress comes mostly from grid decarbonisation, not their own action.
why: The second point (cause of scope 1-2 decline) is not visible in the chart, so notes add information; rule 4.

prompt: Freight cost per pallet by lane over the last 8 quarters. The Midlands lanes diverged after the Coventry depot closure; annotate that quarter.
why: Time series with a pinned event point; rule 4.

prompt: Attrition by tenure band: <1y 34%, 1-2y 22%, 2-5y 14%, 5y+ 7%. Want to call out that first-year attrition is concentrated in two regions and exit surveys blame onboarding.
why: Chart shows the gradient, but the region and exit-survey points are extra information; rule 4.

prompt: Marketplace GMV vs take rate, 2021-2026. Take rate fell from 14% to 11% while GMV tripled; explain that this was a deliberate trade-off and what it bought us.
why: Two series whose relationship needs explaining; rule 4.

prompt: SME card adoption by company size: adoption jumps at 20+ employees, and I want to note that the under-10 segment still uses personal cards.
why: Data over categories plus an observation the chart cannot show; rule 4.

prompt: Results of the pricing test, conversion by tier: £29 7.1%, £39 6.8%, £49 4.2%, £59 3.9%. Highlight the cliff between 39 and 49 and what it means for how we package plans.
why: Size comparison with a pinned cliff and an implication to explain; rule 4.

prompt: Show UK SME card spend: 2019 £61bn, 2020 £55bn, 2021 £66bn, 2022 £72bn, 2023 £78bn, 2024 £84bn. The message is it recovered and has grown ~8% a year since 2021.
why: A trend a single title explains; rule 5, no notes needed.

prompt: Slide with the NHS elective waiting list since 2015. It's the obvious hockey stick, no commentary needed.
why: Series the title alone explains; rule 5.

prompt: Compare cost per delivery across our carriers: DPD £4.10, Evri £2.90, Royal Mail £3.40, UPS £5.20, in-house £3.80. The point is simply who's cheapest.
why: Comparison of sizes that the title explains; tie-breaker favours chart; rule 5.

prompt: Headcount by function over the last 4 years for the HR review. The message is just that G&A grew faster than every other function.
why: Series whose single message fits in the title; rule 5.

prompt: Unit economics of our three plans side by side (price / gross margin / CAC / payback months): Starter £0 / 42% / £180 / 14; Growth £49 / 61% / £420 / 9; Scale £199 / 68% / £1,900 / 11. Point out Growth is the sweet spot and Scale payback is inflated by enterprise sales cost.
why: Exact mixed-unit figures that need interpretation; rule 6.

prompt: FinBridge vs Pleo, Soldo and Spendesk on FX fee, monthly fee per user and credit line. Then what it means for our positioning.
why: Exact figures across 4 columns with a positioning interpretation; rule 6.

prompt: Store P&L for the four pilot stores: sales, labour %, shrink %. I need to explain why Leeds underperforms despite the best top line.
why: Exact figures, 4 columns, needing interpretation; rule 6.

prompt: Procurement bids: Vendor A £2.1m, 36-month term, 99.5% SLA; Vendor B £1.8m, 48 months, 99.0%; Vendor C £2.4m, 36 months, 99.9%. Board needs the exact numbers and our read on the trade-offs.
why: Reader needs exact values plus interpretation; rule 6.

prompt: Clinical trial site performance for 5 sites: enrolment vs target, screen-failure rate, dropout rate. Call out which sites we should close.
why: Exact figures, 4 columns, with a recommendation to explain; rule 6.

prompt: Four market-entry countries (TAM / licence timeline / competitors): Germany €9bn/12mo/14, France €7bn/9mo/8, Netherlands €2bn/4mo/5, Spain €4bn/10mo/6. We recommend NL first; say why.
why: Exact figures across 4 columns needing interpretation; rule 6.

prompt: This quarter's KPIs vs plan: ARR, NRR, gross margin, each with actual, plan and variance. Need to explain the NRR miss.
why: Exact values (4 columns) with a miss to interpret; rule 6.

prompt: Abatement options with cost per tonne and potential: fleet EVs £45/t 1.2Mt, heat pumps £80/t 0.8Mt, solar PPA -£10/t 2.1Mt, offsets £15/t unlimited. I want to make the case that offsets are a trap.
why: Exact figures with interpretation (rule 6); a cost-curve chart with notes is a defensible alternative.

prompt: Council budget by department, 2025 vs 2026 and % change, six departments. Add notes on which cuts hit statutory services.
why: Exact figures, 4 columns, that need interpretation; rule 6.

prompt: Feature comparison vs 4 competitors across 8 features for the product review, ticks and crosses.
why: 5 columns and 8 rows; rule 7.

prompt: Regional sales pack: 7 regions with revenue, growth, margin and revenue per head. The committee just wants to look the figures up.
why: 5 columns and more than 6 rows, no interpretation; rule 7.

prompt: FinBridge card tiers Free, Plus, Pro, Enterprise with monthly fee, cards included, FX fee and cashback, so the pricing committee can compare.
why: Exact figures across rows, 5 columns; rule 7 comes before cards.

prompt: Workstream status for the steering committee: 8 workstreams with owner, RAG, next milestone and date.
why: More than 6 rows, 5 columns; rule 7.

prompt: Benchmarks for the 10 GP practices in the network: patients per GP, DNA rate, average wait in days. They'll read the numbers themselves.
why: More than 6 rows of exact values the reader looks up, no single visual message; rule 7.

prompt: Three carriers: on-time %, damage rate, cost per parcel, claims paid. The audit committee just wants the numbers, no commentary.
why: Exact figures with 5 columns and no interpretation wanted; rule 7.

prompt: Walk through the 18-month ERP rollout plan: design, build, pilot, rollout, hypercare.
why: A 5-step plan in time; rule 8.

prompt: How a FinBridge expense flows from tap to ledger: card tap, receipt capture, auto-categorisation, approval, sync to Xero.
why: An ordered process, not parallel items; rule 8.

prompt: The client's M&A history: bought Northway in 2016, Cardell in 2019, merged with Vesta in 2022, carved out the services arm in 2025.
why: A history of 4 dated steps; rule 8.

prompt: Our recommended three-horizon roadmap for the retailer's digital transformation: fix the basics (0-6m), scale omnichannel (6-18m), new business models (18m+).
why: Horizons are sequenced in time, so a roadmap; rule 8 before rule 9.

prompt: The patient referral pathway today: GP referral, triage, diagnostics, consultant review, treatment. Want to show where the delays pile up.
why: A 5-step process; rule 8.

prompt: Three strategic options for the board: build organically, acquire a payroll player, or partner with a bank. One line on each.
why: Parallel options; rule 9.

prompt: The four pillars of our people strategy: attract, develop, reward, retain.
why: Parallel pillars, not steps in time, despite the lifecycle ordering; rule 9.

prompt: Headline results from the pilot: 23% fewer stockouts, £1.4m working capital released, 4.2pts margin uplift. Three wins, all of them matter.
why: Several independent numbers of equal weight; rule 9 tie-breaker.

prompt: Contrast how SMEs manage expenses today (shared card, spreadsheets, month-end chasing) with FinBridge (per-employee cards, real-time receipts, auto-reconciliation).
why: A two-way contrast; rule 9.

prompt: Key risks to the programme (data migration, change fatigue, vendor lock-in) and a mitigation for each.
why: Three parallel items; rule 9.

prompt: The case for the transition plan rests on three numbers: £120m carbon tax exposure by 2030, 35% of revenue from high-carbon products, and a 2.1x valuation premium for leaders.
why: Three independent numbers, none decisive alone; rule 9 tie-breaker.
